title: Divisibility by 7 and 13 via Alternating 3-Digit Block Sums
description: Since 1000 ≡ -1 (mod 7) and 1000 ≡ -1 (mod 13), divisibility by 7 or 13 can be tested by computing the alternating sum of 3-digit blocks. Proves the general alternating block rule and instantiates it for 7, 13, 11, and 101.

overview.historicalContext: Divisibility rules have been studied since antiquity. The rules for 3 and 9 (digit sum) and for 11 (alternating digit sum) were well known in medieval Islamic and European arithmetic. The rule for 7 is less famous because 7 does not divide 10ʰⁿ−1 for small n (unlike 9 or 11). The key fact 1000 ≡ −1 (mod 7) appears in 19th-century textbooks as a curiosity. Its unification with the 11-rule (using 10 ≡ −1 mod 11) and 13-rule (using 1000 ≡ −1 mod 13) into a single general theorem is a clean result of modern modular arithmetic. The surprising connection: 7 × 11 × 13 = 1001, so 1001 ≡ 0 (mod 7,11,13), making 1000 ≡ −1 modulo all three simultaneously.
overview.problemStatement: Given the congruence $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$ (and $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{13}$), prove that divisibility by 7 (resp. 13) can be tested by the alternating sum of 3-digit blocks: $7 \mid n \iff 7 \mid (a_0 - a_1 + a_2 - \cdots)$ where $n = a_0 + a_1 \cdot 1000 + a_2 \cdot 1000^2 + \cdots$. Generalize to: for any $d$ and base $b$ with $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$, the same alternating block sum tests divisibility by $d$.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof has two steps. First, prove $n \equiv \text{altDigitSum}(b, n) \pmod{d}$ by induction on the base-$b$ digits (using `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` from the parent file `DivisibilityRules`). Second, convert the congruence into the divisibility biconditional: if $n \equiv s \pmod{d}$, then $d \mid n - s$, so $d \mid n \iff d \mid s$. Both directions use `dvd_add` with the congruence.
keyInsights: 1000 ≡ -1 (mod 7) is the single fact that enables 3-digit block alternating sums to test divisibility by 7; it follows from 7 × 143 = 1001 = 1000 + 1.
The same base (b=1000) works for both 7 and 13 because 7 × 13 = 91 divides 1001, making 1000 ≡ -1 modulo both simultaneously.
The general theorem unifies: div-by-11 (b=10, single digits), div-by-7 and 13 (b=1000, 3-digit blocks), and div-by-101 (b=100, 2-digit blocks) into a single framework.
The biconditional proof pattern — using dvd_add with a congruence and its symmetric form — cleanly handles both directions without case analysis.

The alternating sum direction (rather than plain sum) arises from 1000 ≡ -1, not +1. A divisibility rule for a prime d via plain block sum (b ≡ +1 mod d) gives digit-sum-like rules (as for 3 and 9 with base 10), while b ≡ -1 gives alternating sums. The sign alternation encodes the zig-zag structure of the -1 exponents: (−1)^k = (b^k) / b^k → alternating pattern.

sections.title: Module Header: Imports, Open Commands, and Setup
sections.summary: Module docstring explains the OQ-02 question: prove divisibility rules for 7 and 13 via the alternating 3-digit block sum. Imports Proofs.DivisibilityRules (parent file providing altDigitSum and modEq_alternating_digits_sum). Opens BigOperators and Nat; enters DivisibilityRulesOQ02 namespace.
sections.mathContext: The parent `DivisibilityRules.lean` defines `altDigitSum (b n : ℕ) : ℤ` as the alternating sum of base-b digits and proves `modEq_alternating_digits_sum : n ≡ altDigitSum b n [ZMOD d]` whenever `b ≡ -1 [ZMOD d]`. OQ-02 uses this as its key lemma.

sections.title: Part I: Key Congruence 1000 ≡ -1 (mod 7)
sections.summary: Proves 1000 % 7 = 6 by native_decide. This is the single arithmetic fact that enables the 3-digit block alternating sum rule.
sections.mathContext: `one_thousand_mod_seven : 1000 % 7 = 6` — proved by `native_decide`. Since $6 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$, this means $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$, which is the key congruence. Equivalently: $7 \times 143 = 1001 = 1000 + 1$, so $1000 = 1001 - 1 \equiv -1$. In `Int.ModEq` notation: `(1000 : ℤ) ≡ -1 [ZMOD 7]`, which is what `seven_modEq_altDigitSum_1000` uses to apply `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` from the parent.

sections.title: Part II: Divisibility by 7 and the General Rule
sections.summary: Proves seven_modEq_altDigitSum_1000 (n ≡ altDigitSum 1000 n mod 7) and the general dvd_iff_dvd_altDigitSum theorem for any d,b with b ≡ -1 (mod d). Instantiates to seven_dvd_iff_altDigitSum.
sections.mathContext: `seven_modEq_altDigitSum_1000 (n : ℕ) : (n : ℤ) ≡ altDigitSum 1000 n [ZMOD 7]` — from `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` in the parent, instantiated at `b = 1000` and the congruence $1000 \equiv -1 \pmod{7}$. **General theorem** `dvd_iff_dvd_altDigitSum (d b n : ℕ) (h : b ≡ -1 [ZMOD d]) : d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ altDigitSum b n` — proof: $n \equiv \text{altDigitSum}(b, n) \pmod{d}$, so $d \mid n - \text{altDigitSum}$ and $d \mid n \iff d \mid \text{altDigitSum}$ by `dvd_add`. `seven_dvd_iff_altDigitSum`: instantiate at $d = 7, b = 1000$ using the proved congruence.

sections.title: Part III: Divisibility by 13 via Alternating 3-Digit Blocks
sections.summary: Proves 1000 ≡ -1 (mod 13) and derives the divisibility test for 13 using the same 3-digit block sum as for 7.
sections.mathContext: `one_thousand_mod_thirteen : 1000 % 13 = 12` — proved by `native_decide`. Since $12 \equiv -1 \pmod{13}$: $13 \times 77 = 1001 = 1000 + 1$. The same base $b = 1000$ works for both 7 and 13 because $\text{lcm}(7, 13) = 91$ divides $1001 = 7 \times 11 \times 13$, making $1000 \equiv -1$ modulo $7, 11, 13$ simultaneously. `thirteen_dvd_iff_altDigitSum (n : ℕ) : 13 ∣ n ↔ 13 ∣ altDigitSum 1000 n` — proved by `dvd_iff_dvd_altDigitSum` at $d = 13, b = 1000$.

sections.title: Part IV: Concrete Examples and Classical Instances (11, 101)
sections.summary: Concrete native_decide examples for 7. Derives eleven_dvd_iff_altDigitSum (classical rule, b=10) and hundredone_dvd_iff_altDigitSum (b=100). Summary section lists all proved results.
sections.mathContext: Concrete examples verified by `native_decide`: $7 \mid 1001$ (altDigitSum$(1000, 1001) = 1 + 1 = 2$... wait, $1001 = 1 \cdot 1000 + 1$, so altDigitSum $= 1 - 1 = 0$, $7 \mid 0$ ✓). **Classical instances**: `eleven_dvd_iff_altDigitSum`: $b = 10$, since $10 \equiv -1 \pmod{11}$; the alternating 1-digit sum rule (alternating digit sum divisible by 11). `hundredone_dvd_iff_altDigitSum`: $b = 100$, since $100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$; the 2-digit block alternating sum rule for 101. These show the general framework covers all classical alternating divisibility rules, unified by $b \equiv -1 \pmod{d}$.

conclusion.summary: Proves a general alternating block divisibility test: for any d and base b with b ≡ -1 (mod d), divisibility by d is equivalent to divisibility of the alternating sum of b-ary blocks. Instantiated for d ∈ {7, 11, 13, 101} with respective bases b ∈ {1000, 10, 1000, 100}.
conclusion.implications: The framework shows that divisibility rules for 7, 11, 13, and 101 are all instances of a single pattern determined by the congruence b ≡ -1 (mod d). More generally, b^k ≡ -1 (mod d) yields a k-digit alternating block sum rule. This unification suggests a complete classification of 'alternating sum' divisibility rules for all d.
openQuestions: Classify all d for which there exists b and k with b^k ≡ -1 (mod d) — these are exactly the d for which the multiplicative order of b modulo d is even.
Derive a divisibility rule for d=7 using a different approach: since 10^6 ≡ 1 (mod 7), a 6-digit cyclic sum rule exists. Compare the efficiency of the two approaches.
Extend to divisibility rules in bases other than 10 (e.g., hexadecimal: 16^k ≡ -1 (mod d) for which d?).

crossReferences.description: The parent divisibility rules collection — provides `modEq_alternating_digits_sum` and `altDigitSum` that this entry imports directly. The parent file proves the general modular arithmetic foundations; this entry applies them to the specific case b ≡ -1 (mod d) and derives the alternating block sum tests for 7, 11, 13, and 101.

OQ-01 on extensions with truncation, grouping, and casting-out-nines. Together OQ-01 and OQ-02 cover the main classical divisibility tests: OQ-01 handles additive (b ≡ +1) and truncation approaches, OQ-02 handles alternating (b ≡ -1) block sum rules. The unification in OQ-02 (all d with b ≡ -1 mod d) complements OQ-01's digit-sum rules (d | 9 or d | b-1 gives digit sum tests).

The classical divisibility-by-3 rule (digit sum divisible by 3, since 10 ≡ 1 mod 3) is the b ≡ +1 analog of the alternating sum rules here (b ≡ -1). Both exploit the congruence of the base modulo the divisor — the sign difference (≡ +1 vs. ≡ -1) determines whether plain sums or alternating sums are used. The connection 7×11×13=1001 explaining why 1000 ≡ -1 mod 7,11,13 simultaneously parallels 9×...=999 patterns used for digit-sum rules.

General Truncation Divisibility Rule — the complementary approach where divisibility is tested via a truncation procedure rather than block sums. For 7, both a truncation rule (double last digit, subtract) and the 3-digit alternating block sum rule (this entry) exist. The two methods reflect different decompositions of 7's relationship to powers of 10, and can be proven to be equivalent via modular arithmetic.
